prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, in which neutral atoms trapped at a magic wavelength enable frequency standards with fractional uncertainties near 1e-18

statement.case_for: I keep a single-part prize for optical lattice clocks. After the full first round my reasons are sharper, not merely repeated. The magic-wavelength condition is a specific, original idea: it cancels the lattice light shift on the clock transition while many atoms sit in the Lamb-Dicke regime, which is what let neutral-atom clocks combine the stability of large ensembles with the accuracy of trapped ions. Katori proposed it and built the first strontium lattice clock; Ye's laboratory then drove accuracy and stability to the 1e-18 regime and opened many-body and spin-correlation physics in the lattice. Several species and several independent laboratories now reproduce this level, and intercomparisons agree. That is the maturity test I apply, and B007 passes it more clearly than any other candidate. I also note the chair's observation that several colleagues moved to B007 after the openings; I do not count that as merit and rest my own view on the scientific record. The credited pair maps onto the idea and the decisive realisation, which is the cleanest attribution on the shortlist. I would word the citation around neutral-atom lattice trapping at the magic wavelength, so that what is rewarded is distinct from the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 prize for control of single trapped quantum systems.
statement.case_against: The reservations that remain are real. Precision metrology has been honoured in 1997, 2005 and 2012, and a clock prize can be read as another step along that lineage. The most consequential application, a redefinition of the second, has not yet happened, so part of the payoff is prospective. Uncredited contributors, in particular Takamoto, Ludlow, Lemonde and Lisdat, and the PTB, SYRTE and NIST groups, have legitimate claims that a two-name citation cannot capture; Ye's group in particular did not work alone in the comparisons. Against these points, the lattice concept is separable from combs and ion control, and the two-name limit is a constraint of the prize, not evidence that the work is weak. I weigh the metrology-lineage concern as a question about citation wording and not as a reason to prefer a less mature candidate.

responses.point: In round 1 Eriksson argued that eight years of replication and extension to other moire systems make magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene timely, not premature, and that moire quantum matter has no prize of its own whereas B007 sits in a corridor honoured in 2005 and 2012.
responses.response: I accept the correction on timing: eight years of replication and a large theory-experiment literature make B005 timely, and my phrase 'arguably early' in round 1 was too strong. My preference remains with B007 for three reasons. First, the overlap argument concerns what the citation rewards. A neutral-atom magic-wavelength lattice is a different invention from a comb or from single-ion quantum logic, so the corridor is not the same achievement. Second, you concede that the pairing mechanism is unresolved and that Cao, the first author of the 2018 experiments, cannot be named from the supplied credits. That is a credit problem specific to this candidate and a three-name limit cannot repair it; a prize that omits the first experimental author invites the kind of dispute we would not face with Katori and Ye. Third, the intrinsic-versus-disorder question is still open for the superconducting state. If the committee wants B005, I would support the citation limited to the flat-band prediction and the observation of correlated insulating and superconducting states, with no claim on mechanism, but it does not change my first choice.

responses.point: Danielsson moved to B005 as a first choice because it pairs a precise theoretical prediction (Bistritzer-MacDonald, 2011) with an experimental discovery in 2018 that many laboratories reproduced, and because it appears in the top four of all eight opening ballots.
responses.response: The theory-prediction plus decisive-experiment structure is a strong criterion and I agree it is B005's best feature. B007 has the same structure in a different form: Katori's magic-wavelength proposal was followed by the experimental clock, and the accuracy was then confirmed by independent groups at 1e-18. I weigh the broad appearance in all eight top-four lists less than you do, since it partly reflects B005 being the safest second choice for many members, not a first choice for most. Where I take your point seriously is that three credited names are defensible, and that the Cao omission may be a recurrent effect of the three-name limit and not a disqualification. I still prefer to reward the achievement whose credited pair has no principal claimant missing and whose reproducibility is established, and I would revisit B005 in a few years when mechanism and credit have settled.

responses.point: Kroll supports a two-name B007 prize with the citation worded around neutral-atom lattice trapping at the magic wavelength, opposes adding a third name, and stresses Ye's contribution beyond the first demonstration.
responses.response: I agree on both wording and attribution. Adding a third name would force a choice among Takamoto, Ludlow, Lemonde and Lisdat that no argument I know of can make non-arbitrary, and Katori plus Ye maps onto the concept and the record-accuracy programme. Your Boulder background with the comb work is the relevant disclosure and I do not see a bearing on the lattice-clock credit. I would go slightly further on one point: the citation should name the invention and its realisation at the 1e-18 level, not the redefinition of the second, since the latter has not happened and should not be implied as part of the achievement.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, calls B007 the one candidate where an original idea became a working instrument reproduced by many laboratories, but warns that if the committee judges B005 more transformative, B007 is the natural runner-up, and notes that ion-clock and lattice-clock groups have legitimate claims.
responses.response: I agree that B005 is the real competitor and that scale is its strength. I do not accept that scale decides the matter when two of the chair's own questions, the unresolved mechanism and the missing first author, bear directly on whether we can write a citation we will not later regret. I also accept your point that other groups have legitimate claims; I do not think they change the credited pair, because the prize rewards the concept and the decisive realisation, but the citation should say so plainly. On the chair's question about a two-part prize, I do not see a second part that is distinct enough from B007 and B005 to add without blurring attribution, and I would not add one merely to broaden field coverage.

responses.point: Mehlig argued that B007 is the most defensible configuration on originality, attribution and maturity, but flagged that the redefinition of the second is pending and that uncredited contributors would be hard to defend, and was more cautious than I about B041 for its four names and overlap with B031.
responses.response: I agree with your caution on B041: four credited names for three places, with Cirac's theory overlapping B031, would make the attribution contested, and the quantum-simulation programme is still maturing. I have therefore kept B041 only as a lower alternative. On the pending redefinition, I would not treat it as a reason to wait, because the claim for B007 rests on demonstrated 1e-18 accuracy and independent reproduction that already exist, and the redefinition is a consequence, not the discovery.

uncertainties: Whether the pending redefinition of the second, if it were to slip, would weaken the public case for B007 even though the scientific claim rests on demonstrated accuracy.

Whether the committee will accept a citation that separates neutral-atom lattice trapping from the 2005 and 2012 recognitions, and whether Takamoto, Ludlow, Lemonde or Lisdat should alter the view of a two-name prize.
How much of B005's unresolved pairing mechanism and credit gap would be mitigated by a narrower citation, and whether I would then rank it first in a later year.
My knowledge of priority history relies on recollection and not on verified records.
statement.conflict_note: My profile documents a long-running collaboration with Anne L'Huillier, papers with the Lund attosecond group, work with Ursula Keller's group at ETH Zurich and other collaborations. None is a documented connection to Katori or Ye, and I know of no specific conflict for B007. As an atomic theorist I may be biased toward AMO topics, which the chair has recorded; I ask colleagues to challenge me on that. I would flag possible recusal only if the committee turned to a candidate involving my named collaborators. No change from round 1.
